noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand the mechanism of the free radical substitution reaction between an alkane and a halogen: i using free radicals, which are species with an unpaired electron, represented by a single dot ii showing the initiation step of the mechanism, with curly half-arrows for free radical formation iii showing the propagation and termination steps of the mechanism iv having limited use in synthesis because of further substitution reactions Further suggested practical Cracking alkanes by thermal decomposition, including liquid paraffin using aluminium oxide as a catalyst

primer.text: Sunlight converts a halogen molecule into radical scissors that snip at alkanes. This note steps through free radical substitution: the ultraviolet initiation that splits the halogen, the two alternating propagation steps that keep the chain running, the collisions that terminate it, and why further substitution spoils clean synthesis.

lessons.title: Initiation: sunlight forges the first radicals
lessons.opening: Every radical chain needs a spark. Ultraviolet light splits the halogen molecule homolytically, and two radicals step out into the mixture carrying single unpaired electrons - the armed and dangerous starters of the substitution story.
keyPoints: The initiation step splits the halogen molecule homolytically under ultraviolet light.
Cl2 -> 2Cl• produces two chlorine radicals, each carrying an unpaired electron.
Free radicals are species with an unpaired electron, represented by a single dot.
The half-headed (fishhook) curly arrow shows single-electron movement in radical mechanisms.
No organic product forms in initiation - it only manufactures the radicals that work later.

low.restatement: UV light snaps the Cl-Cl bond evenly into two chlorine radicals; nothing organic happens yet - the step just loads the gun.
low.analogy: Lightning splits a log into two torches: the fire (reaction) has not started, but the ignition sources now exist.
low.examPointer: Write Cl2 -> 2Cl• with dots and state the UV condition - the equation and the condition are each worth a mark.

medium.restatement: Homolytic fission under UV is the doorway from a stable molecule to two electron-hungry radicals; the fishhook arrows distinguish single-electron movement from the full curly arrows of ionic mechanisms.
medium.analogy: The UV photon is the auction hammer that splits a joint estate into two half-estates, each heir (radical) immediately hunting to rebuild a pair.
medium.examPointer: Do not use ordinary curly arrows here - half-headed arrows are the notation of record for single-electron steps.

check.stem: What happens during the initiation step of free radical substitution?

options.text: The halogen molecule splits homolytically into two radicals
options.explanation: UV energy divides the shared pair evenly.

options.text: A methane molecule loses a hydrogen
options.explanation: That is propagation's business.
Organic product appears only in propagation.
Recombination is termination.

check.stem: Which equation and condition correctly describe initiation?

options.explanation: The canonical initiation of the methane chlorination chain.
That is heterolytic fission.
The UV condition is required.
Methane does not initiate this chain.

check.stem: How are free radicals represented in mechanisms?

options.text: By a single dot showing the unpaired electron
options.explanation: Cl• carries its dot everywhere it appears.
Radicals are neutral.
Radicals are electron-short, not octet-complete.
Dots, not underlines, are the convention.

check.stem: What does a half-headed curly arrow signify in a radical mechanism?

options.text: The movement of a single electron
options.explanation: Half-heads track single electrons; full heads track pairs.

options.text: The movement of an electron pair
options.explanation: That is the full-headed arrow's meaning.
Arrows follow electrons, not atoms.

options.text: The direction of the overall reaction
options.explanation: Arrows are local, not global.

check.stem: Why does initiation produce no organic product?

options.text: It only generates the radicals that later attack the alkane
options.explanation: The halogen split is purely preparative.

options.text: Methane refuses to react at all
options.explanation: Methane reacts in propagation.
Methane is unaffected by UV here.
Radicals are the most reactive species present.

check.stem: Write the initiation step for the chlorination of methane, including the condition.
check.modelAnswer: Cl2 -> 2Cl•, initiated by ultraviolet light splitting the halogen molecule homolytically.

check.stem: Define a free radical and state the notation used for it.
check.modelAnswer: A free radical is a species with an unpaired electron, represented by a single dot after the symbol.

check.stem: Explain why ultraviolet light is required for initiation but not for the propagation steps.
check.modelAnswer: Breaking the Cl-Cl bond homolytically needs the photon's energy input, whereas the propagation reactions release energy through new bond formation and run spontaneously once radicals exist.

check.stem: Bromine is used instead of chlorine in a radical substitution. Write the initiation step with correct notation and name the condition.
check.modelAnswer: Br2 -> 2Br• under ultraviolet light: the halogen molecule splits homolytically into two bromine radicals, each carrying its unpaired electron as a dot.

lessons.title: Propagation: the chain that feeds itself
lessons.opening: Propagation is a two-stroke engine of chemistry: the chlorine radical strips a hydrogen from methane, and the methyl radical formed strips a chlorine from Cl2. Each stroke regenerates the radical the next stroke needs, so the chain runs on and on.
keyPoints: Propagation step one: Cl• + CH4 -> CH3• + HCl, the radical extracting hydrogen.
Propagation step two: CH3• + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + Cl•, the chain carrier regenerated.
The two steps alternate indefinitely, which is why propagation is a chain reaction.
Every propagation stroke consumes one radical and produces another - the count never falls.
The overall equation sums the strokes: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl.

low.restatement: A chlorine radical steals H (making HCl and a methyl radical); the methyl radical steals Cl (making chloromethane and returning a chlorine radical) - around it goes.
low.analogy: A relay with two runners (Cl• and CH3•) passing the baton (the unpaired electron) endlessly around the track.
low.examPointer: Write both propagation equations; a single step is half the marks, and the regenerated radical must appear in step two.

medium.restatement: The chain's arithmetic is self-sustaining: radicals consumed equals radicals produced in every cycle, so a single initiation event can spawn thousands of substitution turnovers before any termination collision ends the run.
medium.analogy: A single spark can burn a whole forest: one radical seeds a cascade whose every step forges the next attacker.
medium.examPointer: Sum the two propagation equations to show the overall substitution and cancel the radical intermediates - examiners reward the summed form.

check.stem: Which equation is propagation step one in methane chlorination?

options.explanation: The chlorine radical extracts hydrogen.
That is step two.
That is initiation.
That is a termination collision.

check.stem: Why is propagation called a chain reaction?

options.text: Each step regenerates the radical the next step needs
options.explanation: The carrier is never depleted until termination.

options.text: The reactions happen in a physical chain of molecules
options.explanation: The chain is chemical, not spatial.

options.text: Each step requires fresh UV light
options.explanation: Only initiation needs the photon.
Small molecules only.

check.stem: What does propagation step two regenerate?

options.text: A chlorine radical from chlorine molecules
options.explanation: CH3• + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + Cl• hands the baton back.
Step one, not step two, forms methyl radicals.
Light is consumed, not generated.
HCl is step one's product.

check.stem: Sum the two propagation steps. What overall change do they achieve?

options.text: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl, with radicals cancelling
options.explanation: One hydrogen swapped for one chlorine.
Further substitution is not this sum.
The chlorine must land somewhere as HCl.
That is triple substitution, not one cycle.

check.stem: What happens to the radical count during propagation?

options.text: It stays constant: every stroke consumes one and makes one
options.explanation: Self-sustaining by design.
Growth would runaway-explode instantly.
Decay would end the chain immediately.
Sunlight is not part of propagation.

check.stem: Write both propagation steps of methane chlorination with radical dots.
check.modelAnswer: Step one: Cl• + CH4 -> CH3• + HCl; step two: CH3• + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + Cl•.

check.stem: State what is meant by a chain reaction in this context.
check.modelAnswer: A chain reaction is the alternating propagation sequence in which each stroke consumes one radical and regenerates another, letting the substitution run thousands of times from one initiation event.

check.stem: Explain why the propagation steps' sum equals the overall substitution equation.
check.modelAnswer: Adding the two strokes cancels the radical intermediates - Cl• appears as reactant then product, CH3• likewise - leaving only CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl.

check.stem: Write the two propagation steps for the bromination of methane and sum them.
check.modelAnswer: Br• + CH4 -> CH3• + HBr; CH3• + Br2 -> CH3Br + Br•; the sum is CH4 + Br2 -> CH3Br + HBr with both radicals cancelled.

lessons.title: Termination and the limits of the method
sourceHeadings: Limitations of the free radical mechanism
lessons.opening: Radicals die by meeting each other: termination pairs any two radicals into a single unreactive molecule. But the same hunger that drives the chain also drives further substitution, so the product is never a pure halogenoalkane - the method's built-in flaw.
keyPoints: Termination occurs when any two radicals combine into one single unreactive molecule.
Possible terminations include Cl• + Cl• -> Cl2 and CH3• + CH3• -> C2H6.
Further substitution continues: CH3Cl can lose more hydrogens to give CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4.
The product mixture's variety makes free radical substitution of limited synthetic use.
Multi-carbon alkanes add isomeric mixtures to the problem, since any chain position can be attacked.

low.restatement: Two radicals colliding end the chain (any pair works, giving Cl2, ethane or chloromethane), but before they collide the chain keeps substituting, so mixtures of over-substituted products always form.
low.analogy: The radical dance floor empties only when two dancers pair off, but while they wait they keep swapping partners on the methane - hence the mixture.
low.examPointer: Write at least two termination equations and name one over-substituted by-product (CH2Cl2) for full coverage.

medium.restatement: The synthetic limitation is statistical: the chain cannot choose which hydrogen to take next, so on multi-carbon alkanes every position competes and every substitution level competes - control requires ionic routes instead.
medium.analogy: A dart player who cannot aim: every throw lands somewhere legal, and the board fills with a mixture no single-order reaction would give.
medium.examPointer: When asked why the mechanism has 'limited use in synthesis', cite further substitution AND the mixture of isomers on longer chains - both halves are named by the specification.

check.stem: What ends a radical chain during termination?

options.text: Two radicals combining into one molecule
options.explanation: The two unpaired electrons pair up.
That is propagation.
Light is not needed after initiation.
Chlorine depletion slows but the defining event is radical pairing.

check.stem: Which equation is a valid termination step?

options.explanation: Two methyl radicals pair into ethane.
That is propagation.
That is propagation.
That is initiation.

check.stem: Which products arise from further substitution of chloromethane?

options.explanation: Each successive hydrogen can be replaced.
Ethane comes from radical pairing, not substitution.
No carbon-carbon bond forms by substitution on methane.
Further substitution is the mechanism's flaw.

check.stem: Why is free radical substitution of limited use in synthesis?

options.text: It produces mixtures through further substitution and uncontrolled positions
options.explanation: Purity is unattainable by this route.
The route needs UV light, not catalysts.
It is an alkane chemistry.
Chain reactions are fast; selectivity is the problem.

check.stem: Chlorinating propane gives several monochlorinated products. Why?

options.text: The radical can abstract hydrogen from any carbon of the chain
options.explanation: Positions 1 and 2 both compete.
All positions compete.
No such rearrangement occurs.

options.text: Chlorine adds across a double bond
options.explanation: Propane is saturated.

check.stem: Write two termination equations for the methane chlorination mixture.
check.modelAnswer: Cl• + Cl• -> Cl2 and CH3• + CH3• -> C2H6 (with CH3• + Cl• -> CH3Cl also possible).

check.stem: List the substitution series methane follows under excess chlorine.
check.modelAnswer: CH4 -> CH3Cl -> CH2Cl2 -> CHCl3 -> CCl4, each step replacing one hydrogen.

check.stem: Explain why a single unreactive molecule forms in each termination step.
check.modelAnswer: Each radical carries one unpaired electron, so two radicals together supply exactly one shared pair - their combination forms one complete, paired, therefore unreactive molecule.

check.stem: A termination event pairs two methyl radicals. Write the equation and show that the atom ledger closes.
check.modelAnswer: CH3• + CH3• -> C2H6: the two radicals together carry 2 carbons and 6 hydrogens, and the ethane product holds exactly 2 C and 6 H, so the ledger closes on both sides.

glossary.definition: The UV-driven homolytic split of the halogen molecule that produces the first radicals.
The alternating chain steps that consume one radical and regenerate another while building the organic product.
The collision of two radicals that forms one single unreactive molecule and ends their chains.
The continued replacement of hydrogens beyond the first, giving mixtures such as CH2Cl2 and CCl4.
